body:
I’m a college student. I’ve been using OneNote since high school to take notes. I’ve had the same iPad since then. I tried uninstalling but that didn’t fix it- instead it just locked me out of taking notes on my iPad at all. I tried installing PowerPoint as a workaround but I had to install an older version due to my iPad’s age and it has this problem too. I looked into it online and other people have been having this problem, but most people say it’s been fixed with the newest update. 

Here’s the problem: you pushed the recent update that caused the issue, but then you limited the update that actually *fixes* the issue to IOS 18 and above. Three months ago I could take notes just fine. Now my iPad is apparently obsolete. I don’t know if you can push updates that are compatible with older versions, but if you can, please fix this. title: Poor implementation of access to photos
body:
iOS gives developers better options than what OneNote appears to be using here. An app can present Apple’s private photo picker, where you can choose any photo at that moment without granting the app permanent access to your whole library. Many apps do exactly that.

With Limited Access, an app can also provide a “Select More Photos” / “Manage Photos” button that invokes iOS’s permission screen from inside the app. OneNote apparently isn’t giving you that convenient path—or isn’t handling the modern picker correctly.

So the awkward workflow you’re seeing is not an unavoidable iPhone limitation. It’s largely a OneNote behavior/design issue.

One workaround worth trying is:

Photos → select photo → Share → OneNote

That hands the specific photo to OneNote directly and normally shouldn’t require OneNote to have general access to the photo library.

Otherwise, Full Access is unfortunately the least irritating solution if you frequently insert photos into OneNote.

The note taking ability is made easy by the fact that you can have multiple notebooks. Within each notebook you can have multiple tabs (for a topic or area of interest), and within the tabs you can have multiple pages, each page can be its own little nugget of information. It beats having to save emails and word docs on your computer, then opening each one for the exact info you are looking for. OneNote has its search bar that will search all notebooks for you. No more guessing where I saw that article and/or wishing I had a copy to send to people. Amazing. Love it. Thank you, developers/designers at Microsoft. There is ONE thing I do want to see as a feature enhancement - allow the MOBILE app to allow searching within the page. Currently only the desktop version has the ability to search within the page or within the entire application. UPDATE - there is a SECOND feature that is missing that’s really useful- the ability to add a row to a table, on the mobile app. Easily done on the desktop app but impossible on the mobile app - the moment you hit enter, it creates a new line within the cell of the table and not a new row. 
FIX these two deficiencies and it’ll be a 5-star app.

title: Mac Support
body:
OneNote is phenomenal on my phone and Windows desktop. I use it all the time. The problem is I also have a Mac laptop. OneNote used to work on the Mac, but now is unusable on the Mac because it does not reliably save changes. This means I will type to-do items on the Mac, trust they are stored in my system, and then they are not present on my phone and windows computer. I instead have to use the online version in a browser window on my Mac. While inconvenient, this would be acceptable if the online version were good. However, the online version is missing multiple functionalities, namely the ability to sort tabs alphabetically. I have been using OneNote for years and have hundreds of tabs. Not having them alphabetical is a significant time suck as I am trying to quickly reference important information in a meeting, but cannot find it. I have been working with OneNote so long and so much of my information and GTD system is there that I will continue to use it for now. However, due to their refusal or failure to keep their web and Mac apps up to speed with their Windows apps, I would not recommend OneNote to new users, especially if you anticipate any possibility of having an Apple device someday. I also would not recommend new users start OneNote because if they dropped the functionality of a once useful application (Mac), I do not know what else they will someday decide to drop the functionality on. For example, if the app on my phone stops working, I’ll need to drop OneNote altogether and start the laborious process of transferring all my systems into a new platform.
Summary: great on certain devices, not on others.

title: The iPad Handicap: Why Microsoft Won't Let OneNote Succeed

title: Mobile Must Step It Up To Be Crowned King
body:
First off, 5-stars to OneNote Desktop. Unfortunately, to take the note application throne, users MUST have seamless synch and relatively equivalent capability across desktop AND mobile. As of 6/26/2025, this iOS app doesn't sufficiently hit that target.

I realize that mobile is not Microsoft's wheelhouse and I suspect Apple is not making improvement easier. The reality is that OneNote iOS usability has barely improved in the last 3-5 years.

That said, the starting capabilities of OneNote's features compared to everyone else in the game (Apple, EverNote, Google, Notion, etc.) are unrivaled: desktop UX, backup/revision history {pivotal!!}, Office integration, page linking, format customization, in-app search, files/images, etc. 

Synch has slowly gotten much better, which is massive, but its mobile UX is so severely lacking that I am considering another switch at this point (after migrating from Apple to OneNote). This app still feels like operating a desktop website on mobile and it's crippling for workflow. I have core pages that suffer fatal typing lag, viewing/organizing notebooks is often impossible, major features/options from desktop are inaccessible, cross-platform translatability  to/from any Google/Apple products is a massive chore, they removed the native 'Look Up' function, synching issues are still commonplace (but remedied with superior backup/history options).

At the end of the day, I need my mobile note interface to be as useable as desktop or the entire system crumbles. Apple Notes is far, far superior on mobile but absolute garbage on desktop and  backup/Cloud utilization. We use our phones much more than our CPU and because of  its size/power constraints, the mobile UX/UI bar MUST be proportionately higher to meet user needs. The first company to master both sides of the coin will definitively own the kingdom. 

I look forward to amending this review if this app does improve.
